title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text: Alex Zajichek

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
section: The problem this is trying to solve
text:
The problem this is trying to solve
This is a problem I have been thinking about for several years. Hospitals may have a readmission score when a patient leaves, but that score quickly becomes stale. Care teams then struggle to assemble what has happened after discharge, while quality and executive leaders often see a separate, delayed set of aggregate measures.
Those are not three independent problems. They are different views of the same work.
The readmission risk pool is the group of recently discharged patients who have not yet been readmitted and can still benefit from follow-up. Managing that pool well means knowing who is in it now, what has changed, where attention may be most useful, and how the collective picture affects hospital performance.
The idea began as a proposed way to connect patient-level follow-up with a hospital-wide view. Read the original 2024 article.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
One connected working picture
The platform is meant to support a shared readmission “command center” without forcing every audience into the same screen or level of detail.

Care teams need a current view of which patients remain at risk, what has happened since discharge, and who may need attention today.
Hospital analysts and modelers need room to use local data, existing discharge scores, and methods that reflect the hospital’s population and reasons for readmission.
Quality and executive leaders need the individual patient picture to roll into trustworthy measures of volume, trends, expected readmissions, and operational impact.

The practical value is the connection between those views. A patient-level risk update should not live in a standalone model, and an executive metric should not be detached from the day-to-day work that produced it.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
section: Start with something that already works
text:
Start with something that already works
The Readmission Risk Pool Hospital Implementation is the repository a hospital installs and customizes. It is not itself a fictional project. It includes fictional data and examples so a team can run and inspect a complete working path—from source data through risk updates and history to a web application—before asking for internal approval or connecting sensitive hospital data.
That makes the early conversation concrete. A developer or analyst can evaluate the workflow, see what the app provides, and identify what the hospital would need to change without starting from a blank repository or committing to a predefined vendor tool.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
section: Adopt it one piece at a time
text:
Adopt it one piece at a time
The platform is intentionally designed for incremental implementation. A hospital can keep a working reference path while replacing one locally owned piece at a time.

Run the complete example. Install the Hospital Implementation and exercise the fictional source-to-application workflow.
Choose the deployment path. The platform can currently generate and validate a repository prepared for Posit Connect Cloud setup. A supported container target is a planned next step for deployment inside hospital-controlled infrastructure.
Connect hospital data. Write the local SQL or other extraction and mapping logic needed to populate the shared canonical model. Once that mapping passes validation, the rest of the pipeline is designed to continue working unchanged.
Make the risk method local. Begin with an existing discharge score if useful, then update risk throughout follow-up using the hospital’s own data and modeling approach. Use a built-in estimand—the precise quantity a model is asked to estimate—or register another quantity that better matches the hospital’s decisions.

The same principle extends to storage, analytical products, and the application: adopt the reference first, then replace a component when there is a concrete reason to do so.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
section: Current risk, not only discharge risk
text:
Current risk, not only discharge risk
The methodological idea is straightforward: risk should reflect what is known now, not only what was known when the patient left the hospital.
A hospital can retain its existing discharge risk score as a useful starting point. During follow-up, its own models can incorporate information such as completed visits, medication access, transportation, or other locally meaningful events. Because different hospitals and patient populations may have different drivers of readmission, the platform does not prescribe one universal model.
It does insist on clarity about what the model predicts. For example, a care team may need the probability that a patient who has not yet returned will be readmitted during the remaining follow-up window—not a generic score whose meaning changes from one implementation to another. That statistical discipline is built into the workflow while leaving the modeling method under hospital control.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
Rigor in the background
There is substantial engineering beneath the working example, but a hospital should not need to understand every internal detail to evaluate or operate it.

Validation is built throughout the workflow so incompatible data or configuration can fail early and visibly instead of silently producing a misleading result.
The normal operator journey is documented through a small set of top-level commands for setup, readiness checks, platform runs, history, product refreshes, application checks, and deployment-artifact generation.
AI and agent workflows are optional conveniences. Every supported operation has a documented human path, and an agent can only invoke the same predefined operations a person can run directly.

The backend documentation remains available for teams that need to review the statistical definitions, validation behavior, history, or replacement boundaries in depth.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
Open source and hospital owned
The Platform and Hospital Implementation are released under the Apache-2.0 license. There is no proprietary platform license required to use, inspect, or adapt the software; a hospital still bears its own implementation, infrastructure, security, and operating costs.
The hospital owns its data connections, model choices, infrastructure, workflows, and local modifications. CentralStatz provides an inspectable foundation rather than a closed tool that dictates how readmission risk must be modeled everywhere.

title: Readmission Risk Pool Platform
text:
Where it stands today
The current release demonstrates a complete, runnable implementation using synthetic data and an intentionally nonclinical reference risk method. It includes durable risk history, analytical products, a web application, strong validation, and generation of deployable application artifacts.
It is not yet a clinically validated or production-approved hospital system. Real use requires local source mapping, development and validation of an appropriate risk method, approved infrastructure, privacy and security controls, workflow design, monitoring, and clinical governance. Posit Connect Cloud preparation is implemented; a supported container target and turnkey inside-the-firewall deployment are not.

Why this exists
Recurring reports often accumulate manual steps, hidden decisions, and formatting work. This project explores a more explicit system: defined inputs, repeatable transformations, a consistent artifact, and clear places for analyst review.

Structure Before Sophistication
Most analytical problems do not begin with dashboards or models. They begin with questions. CentralStatz works through the structure behind the problem before building a solution.
Many organizations focus on output first. The stronger foundation is the system and reasoning that make an output trustworthy: transparent definitions, reproducible processes, defensible metrics, and maintainable implementation.

Meet Alex Zajichek
Alex is a statistician and data scientist in Central Wisconsin with more than a decade of experience learning, teaching, and doing data science work across tools, methods, and problem contexts.
His work is especially grounded in healthcare, where messy systems, consequential decisions, and fragile metrics make sound analytical structure essential. Through CentralStatz, he helps organizations build reproducible analytics, strengthen statistical reasoning, and create systems that make complex questions easier to answer over time.

AI-assisted development can reduce the distance between a well-reasoned concept and a working interface. More importantly, lower implementation cost expands the set of solutions worth considering before one structure becomes expensive to replace.

Structure Before Sophistication
Sophisticated-looking outputs are becoming easier to generate. Framing, definitions, assumptions, architecture, and validation are not.
Expanded technical capability does not make complexity inherently better. A simple method is still the right method when it matches the question, data, and decision. Structure decides where added machinery earns its place—and where it does not.


Clear questionsLet the actual question—not inherited machinery—set the boundary.


Defensible logicMake metrics and assumptions open to review.


Reproducible systemsBuild work that can be understood and repeated.


Honest boundariesState uncertainty and limits alongside capability.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
Alex Zajichek

2026-07-02

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
Why this exists
Simulation projects often begin with a domain-sized ambition: simulate the system. That framing has no natural stopping point because more entities, mechanisms, and interactions can always be added in the name of realism.
Flux Estimand begins with a narrower question: What decision is being evaluated, and which counterfactual worlds need to be compared? The goal is to make the scientific and decision target explicit before implementation choices begin to define the project.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
Current hypothesis
An explicit estimand can anchor a simulation around its decision, conditioning state, alternative actions or policies, outcomes, contrasts, and assumptions. A model can then be judged by whether it is sufficient for that comparison—not by whether it reproduces an entire domain.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
How the framework works

Identify the decision and the moment at which it is made.
Define the shared conditioning state from which counterfactual worlds diverge.
Specify the alternative actions or policies.
Define target quantities, contrasts, assumptions, and validation needs.
Build the simplest ModelBundle capable of estimating those quantities credibly.
Add fidelity only when it materially improves the target comparison.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
Estimands and ModelBundles
The estimand is the stable decision specification. A Flux ModelBundle is one executable implementation of it. Multiple bundles may target the same estimand while using different assumptions, state representations, fidelity levels, or computational strategies.
That separation allows the decision question to remain fixed while implementations evolve or are compared.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
Relationship to Flux
Flux Estimand is owned by Alex Zajichek and is being developed as a methodological layer for decision-oriented applications of Flux. Flux remains a separate simulation ecosystem maintained in its own repository; Flux Estimand does not replace or claim ownership of it.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
What currently exists
The public repository contains conceptual documentation, guidance for creating and reviewing estimands, and a copyable project structure centered on an authoritative ESTIMAND.md. It is a framework repository—not itself an estimand project—and therefore does not contain a root estimand or executable simulation bundle.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
Current limitations
Flux Estimand is experimental methodology. Simulation can make alternative worlds executable under stated assumptions, but it does not establish that those assumptions are correct, that a state representation is sufficient, or that the resulting comparison is valid. The framework complements causal-inference thinking; it is not a substitute for established study-design and estimation methods.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
Next experiment
The next useful test is a concrete downstream decision problem. That application can reveal whether the template clarifies the target comparison, prevents unnecessary model scope, separates scientific assumptions from implementation choices, and produces validation requirements that can actually be evaluated.

title: Flux Estimand Framework
text:
Participate
Methodological critique is welcome—especially around conditioning states, counterfactual definitions, model sufficiency, validation targets, and the boundary between estimands and their implementations.

title: Hospital Readmissions Explorer
text:
Why this exists
Public healthcare datasets contain valuable evidence, but useful exploration often requires knowledge of the source, measures, and analytical tools. This project asks whether a carefully bounded conversational layer can lower that interaction cost without pretending the underlying complexity has disappeared.

title: Hospital Readmissions Explorer
text:
Current hypothesis
A constrained interface can shorten the path from a question to an inspectable result while keeping source data, definitions, and analytical logic visible enough to question.

title: Hospital Readmissions Explorer
text:
What the prototype demonstrates

A custom web interface for asking questions about Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program data.
A deployment path connecting a conversational interaction to analytical output.
A tangible interface that can now be evaluated instead of discussed only as a specification.

title: Hospital Readmissions Explorer
text:
AI’s role
AI-assisted implementation made it faster to connect the interface, analytical workflow, and deployment pieces. It did not define valid measures, determine appropriate interpretations, review the source data, or validate whether a response is fit for a healthcare decision.

title: Hospital Readmissions Explorer
text:
What remains expert-driven
Question framing, measure definitions, analytical constraints, evaluation, interpretation, and governance remain human responsibilities. In this context, a plausible answer is not the same as a defensible one.

title: Hospital Readmissions Explorer
text:
Latest meaningful update
A deployment pipeline and custom web interface were assembled for interactive exploration of HRRP results. The next phase is less about adding surface-level capability and more about testing the structure: which questions are supported, how results expose their basis, and where the interface should decline to answer.
